::: {.lead}
*Pocket Quest 1.0* is finished and tested. Now *Byte Bay* must bring it to
the players, through Google Play and the App Store. A store is not a shelf
where anyone puts anything: it asks for an account, a package with a new
build number, a listing with pictures and texts, an age rating, a privacy
policy, and a review before the game goes live. In lecture 7 you compared
the two platforms. In this lesson you follow the whole road from a build to
the players, and you learn what each store requires at each step. Every
section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary app-store developer-account store-listing build-number age-rating privacy-policy app-review staged-rollout >}}

## 8.1 The road to the store

Publishing has six steps, and each one can stop the launch (@fig-road). The
first step costs money: each store asks for a **developer account**
(@fig-pub).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.1 — The publishing steps"}
1. **Account:** a developer account in each store: Google Play Console
   (about 25 USD once) or the Apple Developer Program (about 99 USD every
   year).
2. **Build:** the package (`.aab` for Google Play, `.ipa` for the App
   Store) with a new build number.
3. **Listing:** the **store listing**: name, icon, screenshots, texts,
   category.
4. **Rating and privacy:** the age-rating questionnaire, a privacy policy
   and a form about the collected data.
5. **Review:** the store checks the game.
6. **Release:** to all players, or step by step.

Both stores keep a share of each sale (often 15–30 %).
:::

![The road from a build to the store.](images/road-to-store.png){#fig-road width=94%}

![Accounts, review and the store's share. Round numbers checked in 2026.](images/publishing.png){#fig-pub width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.1 — Byte Bay's plan"}
1. Three weeks before the launch: the accounts are opened (the identity
   check can take some days).
2. Two weeks before: the final build, screenshots and texts; the rating and
   privacy forms.
3. In the last week: the review (hours to a few days); the release on the
   day of the launch post.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.2 — The accounts for one year"}
1. Android only: 25 USD, once.
2. iOS only: 99 USD, and 99 USD again every year.
3. Both stores in the first year: 25 + 99 = **124 USD**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Opening the accounts one day before the launch. Identity checks and the
first review can take days: start weeks before.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Plan the road"}
Write the six steps for your own small game, with one thing you must
prepare for each step.

*Your result:* a list of six steps.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "1. Account: a Google Play account (25 USD). 2.
Build: the .aab with a new build number. 3. Listing: a short name, an icon,
four screenshots of the real game. 4. Rating and privacy: the questionnaire
and a privacy policy page. 5. Review: send it two weeks before the launch.
6. Release: first to a small part of the players." Check: six steps in this
order, and one real thing to prepare for each.
:::
:::

## 8.2 The store listing

The listing is the shop window of the game. Each store asks for the same
parts, with its own names and limits (@fig-listing).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.2 — Store listing"}
A **store listing** has: an **app name** (short: each store has a limit);
a short text (Google Play: short description; App Store: subtitle); a long
description; an **icon**; **screenshots** of the real game; a category and
contact details. The store's form shows the limits of each part, and its
help pages list them: check them before a launch, because they change.
:::

![A store listing and its parts.](images/listing-parts.png){#fig-listing width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.3 — A name that is too long"}
The studio types "Bee Farm: Grow and Sell the Biggest Vegetables" (46
characters). The store refuses it: the name is over the limit. The studio
writes "Bee Farm" (8 characters) and moves the rest to the short text:
"Grow and sell the biggest vegetables!"
:::

{{< sim file="sims/listing-builder.html" poster="sims/listing-builder.png" title="Store Listing Builder: is Pocket Quest ready?" height="780" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Screenshots of a better-looking game, or of features that do not exist. A
misleading listing is one of the most common reasons for a rejection.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Make the listing ready"}
1. In **Store Listing Builder**, fix every problem for Google Play.
2. Switch to the App Store. Which line becomes a problem, and why?

*Your result:* two ready checklists and one answer.

::: {.check}
For Google Play: a short name such as "Pocket Quest", the icon the form asks
for (512 × 512), 2 or more screenshots, the questionnaire done, a privacy
link and a higher build number. On the App Store the **icon** becomes a
problem: Apple asks for a bigger icon (1024 × 1024). Each store has its own
limits: read them in its form.
:::
:::

## 8.3 Versions, age rating and privacy

Behind the listing, the store checks which version the build is, who may
play the game, and which data it collects (@fig-ver).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.3 — Build number, rating, privacy"}
- **Build number** (Android: version code): it must grow with every upload.
  Players see a **version name** such as 1.0.1.
- **Age rating:** the studio answers a questionnaire (violence, language,
  purchases, chat); the rating follows from the answers.
- **Privacy:** a link to a **privacy policy**, and a form about the data
  (Google Play: Data safety; App Store: privacy labels).
:::

![The version name and the build number.](images/version-numbers.png){#fig-ver width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.4 — Version 1.4.1 of Bee Farm"}
1. The studio fixes a bug: the version name goes from 1.4 to **1.4.1**.
2. The build number goes from 27 to **28**. With 27 again, the upload
   fails.
3. The game still collects no personal data, so the privacy form stays the
   same.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Answering the age-rating questions with "no" to get a lower age. A wrong
rating can remove the game from the store later.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Rate a game"}
Choose a game you know. Answer for it: Does it have violence? Bad language?
Purchases? Chat with strangers? Which age group would you expect?

*Your result:* four answers and an age group.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "Cartoon fights: yes; bad language: no;
purchases: yes (gems); chat with strangers: no. I expect a rating for about
12 and older." Check: four yes-or-no answers, and an age group that fits
them (more violence or open chat gives a higher age).
:::
:::

## 8.4 Review and release

Before the game goes live, the store checks it. Before and after the
review, a studio gives the game to players in steps, so that few players
meet a bug (@fig-release).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.4 — Review, testing tracks, staged rollout"}
The **app review** checks every new game and update against the store's
**guidelines**. Most rejections come from a few problems: crashes, an
incomplete build ("coming soon"), a misleading listing, or a missing
privacy policy. Before the public launch, **testing tracks** give builds to
small groups (internal, closed and open tests; on iOS, TestFlight). After
approval, a **staged rollout** gives a new version to a small part of the
players first, then to more, then to all.
:::

![Testing tracks and a staged rollout.](images/release-tracks.png){#fig-release width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.5 — Version 1.5 of Bee Farm"}
1. Closed test: 20 testers play version 1.5 for one week.
2. Review: approved in one day.
3. Staged rollout: a small part of the players gets 1.5 first. The game
   crashes on phones with 3 GB of RAM: the studio stops the rollout, fixes
   the bug and sends 1.5.1.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Releasing an update to all players at once on a Friday night. If there is a
bug, everyone meets it, and nobody is there to fix it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A release plan"}
Write a release plan for version 1.2 of Pocket Quest: which testing track,
how long, and which steps of the release.

*Your result:* a plan of three to five lines.

::: {.check}
A good plan looks like: "1. Closed test with 20 testers for one week. 2.
Review, sent on Monday. 3. Staged rollout: a small part of the players
first. 4. If the crash rate stays low, more players, then all. 5. If it
rises: stop, fix, send 1.2.1." Check: a testing track with a time, the
review, a release in steps, and what to do if a bug appears.
:::
:::

## Case study: Launch Day

Byte Bay publishes *Pocket Quest 1.0* on Google Play and the App Store. On
launch day it needs a developer account first; then the upload fails
because the version code 12 was used before; the store refuses the app name
"Pocket Quest: The Lost Island of the Seven Golden Keys" (54 characters);
the listing shows screenshots of a different art style; the age rating
must be decided; the review rejects the game for a missing privacy policy;
and version 1.1 needs a safe release. The Game challenge of the interactive
lesson uses this day. In the mini-game below you solve each problem.

## Further reading

Google Play Console Help, "Create and set up your app" and "Prepare your
app for review"; Apple Developer, "App Store Connect Help: Submit an app"
and "Choosing a membership". Check the date on each page: fees and limits
change.

## Exercises

1. Name the six steps of publishing a game.
2. How much does each developer account cost?
3. Which package does each store want?
4. What does each store ask for in a listing? Name four parts.
5. Why must screenshots show the real game?
6. Version 1.4 had the build number 27. Which number does 1.4.1 need?
7. Who decides the age rating, and how?
8. Which two things about privacy does each store ask for?
9. Name three common reasons for a rejection.
10. What is a staged rollout?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Account, build, listing, rating and privacy, review, release.
2. Google Play: about 25 USD once. Apple: about 99 USD every year.
3. Google Play: .aab. App Store: .ipa.
4. For example the app name, a short text, the icon, screenshots (also the
   long description, category, contact).
5. A misleading listing is rejected.
6. A higher one, for example 28.
7. The studio answers the store's questionnaire; the rating follows from
   the answers.
8. A privacy policy link and a form about the collected data.
9. For example crashes, an incomplete build, a misleading listing, a
   missing privacy policy.
10. A release to a small part of the players first, then to more.
:::
